Power Series and Radius of Convergence

Where does a power series converge, and where does it fall apart?

Inside the radius lies a safe zone. There the series converges even with absolute values. Outside, the terms themselves fail to shrink to zero. Points on the boundary each have their own fate.

For example, think of Wi-Fi in a 🏠 house. It works well inside and drops as you walk away. Right at the door it may or may not connect, so you check case by case.

Prove ∑n=0∞xn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^n∑n=0∞​xn has radius 111 and diverges at both endpoints x=±1x=\pm 1x=±1.

R=1,1n↛0,(−1)n↛0R = 1,\quad 1^n \not\to 0,\quad (-1)^n \not\to 0R=1,1n→0,(−1)n→0
Show proof

  1. At x=0x = 0x=0 the series is 1+0+0+⋯=11 + 0 + 0 + \cdots = 11+0+0+⋯=1, converging trivially (every term except the constant term is 000).

    Now assume x≠0x \ne 0x=0 and apply the ratio test to ∣x∣n\lvert x\rvert^n∣x∣n: ∣x∣n+1∣x∣n=∣x∣\frac{\lvert x\rvert^{n+1}}{\lvert x\rvert^n} = \lvert x\rvert∣x∣n∣x∣n+1​=∣x∣ (at x=0x = 0x=0 this ratio is 0/00/00/0, which is why that case was separated).

    It converges for ∣x∣<1\lvert x\rvert < 1∣x∣<1 and diverges for ∣x∣>1\lvert x\rvert > 1∣x∣>1 (terms grow without bound), so the radius is R=1R = 1R=1.

  2. At the endpoint x=1x = 1x=1 the terms are 1n=1↛01^n = 1 \not\to 01n=1→0, so the series diverges by the divergence test.

  3. At the endpoint x=−1x = -1x=−1 the terms are (−1)n↛0(-1)^n \not\to 0(−1)n→0, so the series diverges by the divergence test as well.

  4. Thus the radius is 111, and both endpoints diverge — the boundary must be decided case by case.
